issues.legal_issue: A survey settlement conducted in an alienated village by a former state is a valid survey settlement under the applicable revenue law when the law deems earlier settlements in alienated villages valid.
material_facts: A survey settlement was conducted in the former state, and land revenue was assessed.
Documents before the court showed the settlement, and the successor government had recognized and acted on it.
issues.conclusion: The prior survey settlement was valid under the Land Revenue Code by virtue of its deeming provision.
issues.legal_principle: Section 216(2) of the Bombay Land Revenue Code validates survey settlements previously introduced in alienated villages as though introduced under that section. Section 216(1) applies the relevant survey-settlement chapters to alienated villages with modifications. The court approved State of Gujarat v. Ibrahim Akabarali, which held that settlements conducted by a former state and recognized, accepted, and acted upon by the successor government could qualify under section 216(2).

predicates.survey_settlement_dispute_in_alienated_v: The proceeding concerns whether a survey settlement in an alienated village is legally valid.
predicates.prior_survey_settlement_conducted: An authority of the former state conducted a survey settlement in the village.
predicates.prior_settlement_recognized_by_successor: The successor government recognized and acted upon the former state's survey settlement.
predicates.prior_survey_settlement_is_valid_under_a: The prior survey settlement is treated as a valid survey settlement under the applicable revenue law.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns a survey settlement in an alienated village, a prior settlement conducted by the former state and recognized by the successor government is treated as valid under the applicable revenue law.

issues.legal_issue: An occupant of formerly alienated land becomes entitled to unreserved trees on that land when a valid survey settlement has been completed and the land becomes unalienated.
material_facts: The lands had been part of a proprietary jagir and became alienated when the jagir was granted.
A survey settlement had been conducted and land revenue assessed in the former state; the settlement was valid under the deeming provision.
After abolition of the jagir, the land became unalienated, and the appellants were in actual possession as occupants.
The trees were part of a private forest, were not in a reserved or protected forest, and had not been reserved for the State at the survey settlement or later.
The court distinguished the earlier case concerning forest land subject to a government notification, where there had been no survey settlement.
issues.conclusion: The appellants became occupants of the land together with the forest trees, and government authorities could not interfere with their dealings with those trees before their rights were affected by later acquisition legislation.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(xviii) and 5(1)(b) of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953, made the relevant jagirdar or qualifying holder an occupant liable for land revenue and entitled to the rights of an occupant. Sections 3(4) and 3(16) of the Bombay Land Revenue Code treat land as including things attached to the earth and define an occupant as a holder in actual possession of unalienated land. Under paragraph 2 of section 40, upon completion of a survey settlement, government rights to trees in unalienated land are deemed conceded to the occupant unless reserved. Section 216(2) deems the former state's survey settlement completed under the Code. Section 9 of the Jagirs Abolition Act did not vest these trees in the State because they had not been specially reserved. State of Gujarat v. Ibrahim Akabarali was approved; U. R. Mavinkurve v. Thakor Madhavsinghji Gambhirsingh was distinguished because it concerned land affected by a forest notification and lacked a survey settlement. State of Gujarat v. Kumar Shri Ranjit Singhji Bhavansinghji was also cited in support of rights in land and things attached to it.

predicates.tree_rights_dispute_after_abolition_of_p: The proceeding concerns rights to trees on land after abolition of a proprietary estate.
predicates.valid_survey_settlement_completed: A valid survey settlement had been completed for the land.
predicates.land_became_unalienated: The land became unalienated after the proprietary estate was abolished.
predicates.claimant_in_actual_possession: The claimant was in actual possession of the land as an occupant.
predicates.trees_attached_to_land: The trees were attached to the land in the claimant's possession.
predicates.trees_not_reserved_for_government: The trees had not been reserved for the government at the survey settlement or later.
predicates.no_later_acquisition_affecting_rights: No later acquisition had taken effect to alter the claimant's rights to the trees.
predicates.occupant_may_deal_with_trees_without_gov: The occupant is entitled to deal with the trees and government authorities may not interfere.

issues.definition: Where a tree-rights dispute follows abolition of a proprietary estate, a completed valid survey settlement, unalienated land, actual possession, unreserved attached trees, and no later acquisition affecting the rights lead to the occupant being entitled to deal with the trees without government interference.

issues.legal_issue: A person who becomes an occupant by operation of law does not thereby receive factual permission to occupy land for purposes of a rule deeming permission to include a concession of tree rights.
material_facts: The appellants claimed occupant status under the provision governing the consequences of jagir abolition.
They argued that this status amounted to permission to occupy the land and therefore included a concession of rights to the trees.
The court found that the asserted permission was a legal consequence of occupant status, not factual permission to occupy.
issues.conclusion: The permission-based argument did not establish the appellants' tree rights; permission for this purpose means factual permission and not the conferral of occupant status by law.
issues.legal_principle: The court interpreted paragraph 3 of section 40 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, which provides for tree rights to accompany permission to occupy land in specified circumstances. It held that this means factual permission to occupy, not the legal status of occupant conferred under section 5(1)(b) of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953.

predicates.tree_rights_dispute_based_on_permission_: The proceeding concerns a claim that permission to occupy land carries rights to trees on it.
predicates.occupancy_status_conferred_by_operation_: The claimant's occupant status arose by operation of law rather than from a factual grant of permission.
predicates.no_factual_permission_to_occupy: No factual permission to occupy the land was granted.
predicates.occupancy_status_alone_does_not_confer_t: Occupant status alone does not count as permission that confers tree rights.

issues.definition: If a tree-rights claim relies on permission to occupy but occupant status arose by law without factual permission, that status alone does not confer tree rights as permission.
